query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition of aluminum (≈2 atomic%) into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, protective alumina (Al2O3) scale without significantly compromising its mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, which exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance leading to rapid oxidation (pesting) during high-temperature air exposure.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by alloying in a minor concentration (approximately 2 atomic%) of aluminum into the equiatomic composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under static conditions (with performance benchmarked using tensile testing at room temperature and at 1000 °C with strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹).
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale formed at the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: The aluminum addition facilitates the formation of a stable, slow-growing protective alumina scale that reduces oxygen diffusion into the alloy, thereby mitigating oxidation (pesting) while retaining the desired mechanical properties in both room- and high-temperature regimes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Al-doped alloy will exhibit significantly lower oxidation (evidenced by reduced scale thickness and oxygen penetration) during 5-hour exposure at 800 °C, while maintaining similar levels of ductility and yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy suffers from rapid oxidation (pesting) in air at 800 °C over a 5-hour exposure, despite having acceptable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys modified by a single minor addition of aluminum, with performance assessed after 5 hours exposure in air at 800 °C and mechanical evaluations at room temperature and 1000 °C (using strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum concentration that balances enhanced oxidation resistance with preserved mechanical properties has yet to be established, and there could be unforeseen interactions among the constituent elements that may affect alumina scale formation and adherence.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast alloy samples: one set of the baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and a second set with approximately 2 atomic% aluminum added. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, evaluate the oxide scale using microscopy (SEM/TEM), perform oxygen depth profiling, and conduct tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via SEM/TEM)
Oxygen penetration depth (using depth profiling techniques)
High-temperature yield strength at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-added samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxygen uptake (i.e., thinner, more continuous oxide scale and reduced oxygen penetration) compared to the untreated alloy, or if their mechanical properties (tensile ductility or high-temperature yield strength) degrade beyond acceptable limits, the hypothesis will be falsified.

decision.trend: Early studies on refractory high‐entropy alloys have largely focused on tailoring bulk microstructure – via processing (casting, HIP, SPS) and even minor composition modifications (e.g., Cr addition in Hf‐based systems) – to optimize mechanical properties. In related, non‐equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloys, a single intervention (typically a targeted change to foster the formation of protective surface scales) was successfully used to suppress pesting during moderate high‐temperature (800 °C) air exposure. Although several works have advanced mechanical performance by altering phases or precipitate distributions, none have directly addressed the oxidation/oxygen penetration problem in the equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
decision.unsolved: The critical gap remains the lack of a demonstrated, effective oxidation‐resistance strategy that maintains the beneficial cast microstructure and high mechanical performance at elevated temperatures (800–1000 °C) under air exposure. The earlier techniques that prevented pesting in non‐equiatomic variants have not been transferred to the equiatomic alloy, leaving its surface vulnerability to oxygen unmitigated.
decision.lever: Apply a thin, diffusion‐controlled aluminide (or similar) coating via pack cementation or vapor deposition to induce the in situ formation of an adherent, slow‐growing Al2O3 scale on the as‐cast HfNbTaTiZr surface
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of using targeted surface modifications to form protective oxide layers—a strategy that succeeded in related but compositionally modified alloys—without altering the bulk cast microstructure and mechanical integrity. It is plausible that a controlled aluminizing treatment, optimized in terms of coating thickness and post‐treatment annealing (e.g., 5 h exposure at 800–1000 °C in air under similar mechanical load conditions), will yield an adherent, continuous alumina layer that significantly slows oxygen ingress, thereby preventing pesting while preserving the useful room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance. A controlled experiment demonstrating that a specimen with the coating maintains its strength and ductility after a 5-h air exposure at 800 °C—and conversely, that removal or absence of the coating leads to rapid oxidation—would falsify the hypothesis.
